en: The Sūtra on the Fundamental Non-existence of All Dharmas Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Furthermore, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
There were five hundred members of the assembly and ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas, namely:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Adorned and Polished, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Lion’s Gait,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sovereign King of Unobstructed Flame-Pure Radiance Virtue, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Melody King of Mount Meru’s Peak.
...the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Love-Laughter Immaculate Light, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Radiance Emerging to Overshadow the Sun and Moon,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Supreme Immaculate Crown-Holder, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Majestic Lotus-Blossoming Body,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Brahma-Sovereign Sound, and the Bodhisattva Elephant-Sport...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃharājagati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Suvarṇaprabhāsa-vimalatejas,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mṛdusparśakāya, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Suvarṇālaṃkāravyūhakāya,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śataraśmivimalabala, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śāntendriyeryāpatha.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva Śāntacaryā, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhūmiparamarāja,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva Devabhāṣitagarjitasvara, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Dharmabalavaśitāśāntavihārin,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva Guṇatejo-vimalakāya, and the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Mahāsattvas—these and others, headed by these ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, seeing this assembly of bodhisattvas, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and draped his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over one shoulder. Placing his right knee upon the ground, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and questioned the Buddha regarding the meaning of the Dharma with a verse:
“There is no self, no life-principle, and no nourishing person; Proclaim to me, O One of Boundless Renown, the teaching on these dharmas.”
Tranquil, utterly tranquil, and eternally serene—such is this most excellent assembly.
How can various views be awakening?
How can pride, anger, and envy, as well as the essence of desire, be awakening?
The Guide of boundless renown has taught that if nirvāṇa were non-existent, there would be no freedom from afflictions; how then could the realms of practice be awakening?
Their essence is non-dual, and so it is with the Buddha—O Great Compassionate One, expound this for my sake!
How are all phenomena ultimately liberated? How is their liberation similar to nirvāṇa?
How can they further be equal to space—unimpeded, unattached, and without any point of bondage?
With the voice of a kalaviṅka and the Brahmā-heaven, possessing stainless radiance and the color of golden light;
with pure luminous sound and boundless virtues, you shall preach the Dharma until all dust is extinguished.
How are the various hindrances equal to bodhi?
How is desire the essence of bodhi?
How are dharma and non-dharma, and the path, one—stainless, pure, and equal to space?
If there is neither number nor the absence of number, what is this dharma that has already attained parinirvāṇa?
If there is no awakening and no one who is unattached, how could omniscience also not exist?
In this, there is no contention between the created and the uncreated; grasping and non-grasping both lack intrinsic substance.
Sentient beings have never existed therein, and within these dharmas, there is likewise no obstruction.
Within it there is neither precept nor patience, And likewise, not even a single instance of broken precepts;
In this way, concentration and wisdom are absent, And with the absence of wisdom, wisdom itself is unattainable.
How is this Dharma pure and stainless, Non-existent and equal to space?
When the mind finds no place of attainment at any time, How can there be such a thing as "Dharma" without a mind?
Within this, there is no knowing or seeing; there is no mindfulness, cultivation, or realization, nor is there anything to be abandoned therein.
How is it that sentient beings are identical to the realm of emptiness?
Within this, the essence of phenomena is a single practice; within this, there is neither arising nor transformation.
Neither origination nor birth exists at all—such are the dharmas taught by the Supreme Person.
Within this, there are no learners and no arhats; likewise, there are no pratyekabuddhas.
One who seeks awakening cannot be found; this dharma neither comes nor goes.
Within it there is no abiding and no location, Nor is there going or coming;
Since there is no dharma of coming or going, how could it be Like that Mount Sumeru, standing immovable?
Within this, there is neither perception nor form; how can the essence of form be awakening?
Form and awakening are not two; such is the nature of phenomena as proclaimed by the Supreme Person.
Within this, there is neither emptiness nor signlessness; There is neither attachment nor non-attachment.
How can one speak of dharmas as "named" or "nameless"? To say that the Way is like an echo in the mountains—how so?
Within this, there is neither arising nor affliction, And within this, furthermore, there is no non-arising;
There is nothing already extinguished, nor is there any obstruction— How can all phenomena be said to be a single practice?
Within it there are no devas and no nāgas, no kiṃnaras, yakṣas, and the like;
within it there is no niraya whatsoever, nor any realms of rebirth or sentient beings.

If one speaks of the supreme Dharma of the Teacher, or if one speaks of the various heterodox paths of malicious intent—how can these two be a single practice? How do all such words enter into this oneness?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
How rare, O son of good family!”
"What you have now asked is such that even all the worlds cannot believe or accept it; the worlds of the devas and others shall remain in delusion.
Son of good family!
You need not ask about this causal condition."
O son of good family!
For a beginner bodhisattva, this is not the ground:

namely, those who hold views of emptiness, views of signlessness, views of wishlessness, views of non-arising, views of non-existence, views of the absence of characteristics, views of nirvāṇa, views of the Buddha, and views of awakening.
O son of good family!
This Dharma should not be taught in the presence of a bodhisattva who is a beginner. Why is that?

It is possible that all roots of goodness may be severed; one might then proceed along a path that is not the way to the Buddha's enlightenment, falling into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism, and failing to understand for what purpose or meaning the Tathāgata has taught this Dharma.
When he had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Speak, Bhagavān! Speak, Sugata!"
“World-Honored One!

If there are future bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who hold views of emptiness, views of signlessness, views of wishlessness, views of non-arising, views of non-existence, views of the absence of characteristics, views of nirvāṇa, views of the Buddha, or views of bodhi; who, regarding the sphere of discourse on emptiness and signlessness, become stained by and attached to such discourse, taking words to be pure, claiming that speech is supreme, and valuing fame and profit—”
Having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching on this dharma that is without names, they shall abandon all views and understand that all dharmas are the path of a single characteristic.

According to the faith of sentient beings and according to their faith, they shall skillfully train in the methods of expedient means; although they preach few desires, contentment, and frugality, they do not believe these constitute purity;
and although they speak of the faults and evils of being in the midst of a crowd, they believe in the seclusion of all dharmas.
Although they praise and speak of solitude, uninterruptedness, and non-mixture, they do not believe these constitute purity;
although they praise and speak of generating the bodhicitta, they also know that the self-nature of the mind is itself bodhi;
although they praise and speak of extensively cultivating the sūtras, they believe that all dharmas are themselves extensive.
Although they praise and speak of bodhisattvas, they believe that there is no distinction between śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas;
although they praise and speak of dāna, they skillfully penetrate the equality of dāna;
although they praise and speak of śīla, they skillfully penetrate the intrinsic nature of śīla.
Although he praises and speaks of kṣānti (patience), he thoroughly understands and perceives the dharmas of exhaustion, cessation, and non-arising;
although he praises and speaks of vīrya (diligence), he skillfully discerns all dharmas and does not give rise to them;

although he praises and speaks of dhyāna, samādhi, and samāpatti, and speaks of how samādhi gives birth to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of samādhi-doors, he knows and perceives that their intrinsic nature is samāpanna (absorbed).

Although he has praised the Prajñā through thousands of kinds of characteristics, he has thoroughly mastered both wisdom and non-wisdom, and his essential nature is well-versed in discerning all phenomena.
When he speaks of the faults of desire, he does not perceive a single dharma that can be defiled;
when he speaks of the faults of hatred, he does not perceive a single dharma that can be loathed.
He speaks of the faults of delusion, yet he has faith that all phenomena are free from delusion and unimpeded.
Although he clearly explains to sentient beings the evils of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, he does not perceive the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama as existing.

According to the faith of those sentient beings, they shall teach the Dharma according to that faith; they should have faith in one practice, namely: faith in emptiness, faith in signlessness, faith in wishlessness, faith in non-arising, faith in non-existence, and faith in the absence of characteristics.
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
Please speak it!

Those inconceivable phrases of skillful means are not the domain of any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the first vehicle, with the sole exception of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess deep faith and practice a single path."
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One again addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
"Son of good family!
If that is so, you should listen attentively, reflect with right mindfulness, and I shall explain it for you."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāmin said:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
I shall listen correctly.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to awaken to sublime bodhi, One must not discriminate regarding the faults of desire;
All phenomena are eternally the very nature of desire— Whoever knows this attains the state of the Supreme Honored One."
Greed, hatred, and delusion cannot be found; there is neither one who has already attained them nor one who attains them now.
All phenomena are equal to space; he who knows this attains the state of the Supreme Honored One.
Seeing and not seeing are always of one and the same nature; the Sangha and non-Sangha are two, yet equal as one.
Within this, there is neither Buddha nor sublime Dharma; he who knows this attains worldly wisdom.
Just as a man in a dream, having attained enlightenment, teaches sentient beings;
yet therein is neither a path nor sentient beings—such is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
The seat of enlightenment is unattainable, and that which is unattainable does not exist;
clarity and ignorance—these two are of one single mark. One who knows this becomes a Guide.
It is said that the nature of sentient beings is bodhi, and the nature of bodhi is all sentient beings;
that sentient beings and bodhi are not two different things—those who know this become supreme among men.
Just as a man who skillfully perceives an illusion, That illusion manifests in boundless varieties;
What appears therein is ultimately non-existent, Yet it deludes sentient beings in numbers beyond one.
Greed, hatred, and illusion—each of these afflictions is like a phantom;
ordinary people all think they are stained by passion and anger, yet their deluded and distracted minds lead them toward the evil realms.
Within it there is no greed, hatred, or delusion, nor are there any other afflictions;
having analyzed the nature of phenomena as being like illusions and so forth, the afflictions of ordinary beings are likewise thus.
If there are no afflictions and no sentient beings, Within them there is no Buddha, nor will there ever be;
Having analyzed this dharma of non-arising, The fool thinks, "I shall become a Buddha."
Since there is neither Buddha nor Buddha-dharma, and sentient beings are likewise not to be found anywhere;
if one knows that the essence of phenomena is like empty space, they shall swiftly become the supreme among men.
If one seeks awakening yet lacks true realization, one is as far from awakening as heaven is from earth;
if one knows that the nature of phenomena is equal to an illusion, one shall swiftly become a supreme among men.
If one discriminates regarding precepts, one has no precepts; if one perceives the upholding of precepts, that is breaking the precepts.
That the two—precepts and breaking precepts—are of one single characteristic: he who knows this becomes a teacher.
Just as a man in a dream experiences sensual pleasures and gives rise to joy, Deluded by confused conceptualization, he imagines a woman;
yet within that [dream], the woman is always non-existent.
Breaking the precepts and upholding the precepts are like the nature of a dream; ordinary beings discriminate between these two kinds.
Within them, there is neither precept nor breaking of precept; one who knows this becomes a teacher of the Dharma.
It is known that this is the cognition of ordinary beings, for they do not know the intrinsic nature of sound;
if one realizes that this name is not a name, one shall attain the supreme and wondrous patience.
There are sentient beings who vow to become Buddhas, And proclaim this teaching so that others may know;
Yet they abide in mere words as if it were purity, lacking actual practice— They thereby completely close off the path to Bodhi.
They seize upon errors within the deportments and delight in repeatedly speaking of others' ignorance;
they do not realize bodhi through purity of speech, for they do not know the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Though they constantly proclaim the teaching of emptiness, they take delight in quarreling and harbor malicious intentions;
how can there be awakening or the Buddha-dharma?
Such people merely speak of anger and lack wisdom.
Anger and patience are of one and the same nature; if one knows this, one does not discriminate.
Failing to understand the self-nature of sentient beings, they give rise to all manner of faults and evils—this is the intellect of the ordinary person.
"I myself declare that I love all sentient beings, and as the Supreme Honored One, I shall liberate them.
Yet, when provoked, he immediately gives rise to anger and malice; because of this evil mind, he does not speak with others.
Constantly delighting in strife and seeking out the faults of others, yet praising and speaking of this mind of patience;
likewise preaching that all phenomena are empty, while harboring arrogance within and seeking out errors.
Those who are ignorant and greedily attached to food, day and night contemplate sensual desires;
having entered villages and towns, they say, "I shall liberate all sentient beings."
My compassion turns toward all sentient beings, for I seek their benefit;
though I have clearly explained this nature of the Dharma, they harbor harmful intent and remain constantly malicious.
Yet I have neither heard nor seen anyone who possesses compassion and yet harbors a harmful intent;
having each inflicted wounds upon one another, they now seek the land of Amitāyus.
If there were as many [beings] as the sands of the Ganges River, and one were constantly subjected to insults, humiliation, beating, and abuse;
yet could not endure such evil things, one would not reach that land, O Bull among Men.
If one can know that earth is not earth, then empty earth is like the nature of space itself;
by not conceptualizing earth or the qualities of earth, one shall reach that land, O Bull among Men.
"I claim that I can endure all manner of evils, and I regard the Bodhisattva as my teacher;
yet I have neither heard nor seen any evil arising from regarding him as such."
Each disparaging the conduct of the others, they become attached to the families from whom they beg and to their friends.
Claiming, "These are those I have brought to maturity," they ensure that no other person enters among them.
I am able to liberate you; do not associate with others, for they possess no pure conduct.
To wander amidst the clamor of the crowd is the mark of the ignorant; such people have no share in the benefit of Bodhi.
Thus, throughout the day and night, in three sessions, one should pay homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
do not seek out their faults, but always practice as if wishing to act as a guide for others.
If you see one who delights in the pleasures of sensual desires, do not seek out their faults;
by doing so, you will before long surely realize the supreme enlightenment and its boundless virtues.
One should train gradually and act gradually; Buddhahood cannot be achieved all at once.
For many kalpas, koṭis, and nayutas, I have donned this armor—not just today.
Do not use discrimination to discriminate desire; my contact with bodhi is like the nature of desire.
When these afflictions do not arise, if one can believe this, one attains supreme patience.
Contemplating these various sounds as being non-sounds, one immediately enters the essence of the wordless Dharma;
regarding the essence of all such phenomena categorized as sound, one should give rise to neither desire nor aversion.
In observing desire and hatred as non-arising, one should know that these two have no letters;
these two exist only as the movement of names, for if letters do not exist, they do not exist therein.
If one knows that all words are but a single word, then even names do not arise, for they are fundamentally non-existent;
what I have taught and what the non-Buddhists teach—such categories of dharmic essence they do not understand.
These various dharmas are spoken by means of sounds and words, yet neither dharma nor sound can be apprehended;
being able to enter the path of the single characteristic of all dharmas, one then touches upon and realizes the supreme, unsurpassed patience.
Do not discriminate regarding patience nor lack thereof; do not discriminate regarding anger nor craving.
Constantly understand that these are unarisen, and you shall become a kinsman of the world, supreme among men.
Throughout the eastern, western, southern, and northern directions, there are as many Gaṅgā rivers as there are grains of sand;
if one were to place people upon each single grain of sand, the amount of earth would be boundlessly vast.
If one were to fill the world with various jewels and offer them to the Most Victorious One for more than boundless hundreds of kalpas,
the merit of one who hears this sūtra would be incalculably greater.
Once he has sought this awakening and gone forth as a renunciant, I shall entrust this sutra to him;
he will surely and swiftly attain the most supreme patience, and he shall preach this sutra through its boundless gateways.
Dhāraṇīs will not be difficult for them to obtain; they shall attain millions and billions of sūtras.
They shall acquire sharp wisdom and eloquence; with little effort and vast knowledge, they will swiftly attain liberation.
They shall immediately attain boundless eloquence; all Buddhas will grant them such eloquence.
They shall preach many precious sūtras, and possess boundless eloquence in their discourse.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Virtuous World-Honored One!
How many sentient beings will derive benefit from hearing these verses?"
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
"Son of good family,
do you see this assembly gathered here for discussion?"
He replied: "I have seen them,
Blessed One!"
“I have seen them,
Sugata! They exceed all calculation within this assembly gathered for the teaching of the Dharma.”
Filling the entirety of space, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, and other sentient beings from all other worlds likewise heard this teaching of the Dharma.
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, saying:
"Son of good family!

When this Dharma was being taught, ninety-eight thousand devaputras attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas; ninety-two thousand yakṣas conceived the mind set on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; thirty-six thousand nāgas conceived the mind set on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and five hundred bhikṣus, who were conceited and had not yet attained realization, imagined they had attained it."

Having heard this teaching on the five types of pride and having gained faith and understanding in the single-path nature of all phenomena, their minds were liberated from the outflows because they grasped at nothing.

Among that assembly of bodhisattvas, sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas, having gained faith and understanding in the non-obstruction of all phenomena, attained the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma*).
Why is this? Son of good family!
This Dharma is the most supreme among all teachings.
“Son of good family!

Just as I, in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, attained faith and understanding that all dharmas share the single path of one mark, it was at that time that I subsequently attained patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.”
O son of good family!
Whether one attains the six pāramitās or hears this Dharma-text, they are equal when weighed.
O son of good family!
It is because of this path that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fulfill the six pāramitās;
thus do I speak. Why is this?
"O son of good family!

If there is a bodhisattva who practices giving, guards the precepts, perfects patience, exerts diligence, enters meditative concentration, and cultivates wisdom for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, yet because they do not understand this path of the Dharma, all their roots of goodness will once again be extinguished."
"Son of good family!

Look at Devadatta; he was thus endowed with thirty marks through his possession of such roots of goodness. Yet, despite being so endowed with roots of goodness, he further severed all roots of goodness and consequently fell into the hells, because he did not understand this path of the Dharma."
"O son of good family!
By this causal condition, you should know that those who have severed their roots of goodness do so because they lack knowledge regarding this path of Dharma.
O son of good family!"

In the past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago—further beyond the countless, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, and unfathomable, having passed and further passed—at that time there appeared in the world a Buddha named Meruśikhara-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The lifespan of that Tathāgata is ninety-nine koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand years.
That world is named Golden Flame Reflection; its buddha-field is composed entirely of gold, and it brings sentient beings to nirvāṇa by means of the three vehicles.
What are the three?
They are the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Bodhisattva-yāna.

In that Tathāgata’s first assembly, there were eighty koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand śrāvakas; they were all arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had done what was to be done, accomplished their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and were well-liberated through the knowledge of equality.
In the second assembly, there were seventy koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand bhikṣus.
In the third assembly, there were sixty koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand bhikṣus.

In the fourth assembly, there were twenty-five koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand bhikṣus; twice that number of bhikṣuṇīs gathered; twice that number of upāsakas gathered; twice that number of upāsikās gathered; and twice that number of bodhisattvas gathered.

Those bodhisattvas are fully endowed with the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), skillfully emerge from the path of boundless samādhis, attain the dhāraṇīs of boundless gates, and turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma; how much more so for bodhisattvas who have newly set out on the vehicle?
Within that assembly, there were furthermore immeasurable and innumerable followers of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
O son of good family!
At that time, that Buddha had an immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable multitude of śrāvakas.
“O son of good family!
In that world, Golden Flame Reflection, whether it be trees or pillars, they are all composed of the seven precious jewels.
Those trees produce such sounds as these:”

The sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of non-arising, the sound of non-existence, and the sound of the absence of characteristics—such sounds as these issued forth.
When such sounds as these emerge therein, the minds of those sentient beings are liberated.
After that Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa and his True Dharma has remained for a thousand years, those sounds will no longer emerge.
“Son of good family!

That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Merupradīparāja exhorted the bhikṣu named Viśuddhacāritra to preach the Dharma, and only after he had caused him to preach the Dharma did he pass into parinirvāṇa.”
"O son of good family!

At that time, there was another bhikṣu who preached the Dharma named Sukṛtamatī. He was fully endowed with the aggregate of pure and virtuous precepts and had attained the superior knowledge of the five mundane supernormal powers; he was also able to recite and transmit the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu engaged in rigorous and ardent ascetic practices, and out of faith and delight in frugality, he led a community and expounded the teachings."
Having established a dwelling place, he resides therein;
his followers are well-established in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), taking joy in the qualities of *śrāmaṇera* and practicing austerity;
yet that bhikṣu exerts himself in practice while remaining devoid of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
There are other bodhisattvas who also instruct them in the path of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) to bring them into conformity;

yet they see something to be attained while practicing their teaching, grasping at the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), grasping at the suffering of all conditioned phenomena, and preaching the selflessness of all conditioned phenomena.
They lack skillful wisdom and possess no mastery over the bodhisattva practices.
Although that bhikṣu is thus, he is fully endowed with roots of goodness.

Furthermore, that bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma and practices pure conduct well understands the distinct faculties of each sentient being; his assembly does not value mere quantity of merit or reductionist austerity, but rather excels in the skillful means of the patience of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-kṣānti*).
“O son of good family!

At that time, the bhikṣu Pure Good Practice (Śubhācāra), together with his retinue, arrived at the dwelling of the bhikṣu Good Intention (Sucetanā) and stayed there for the night. Nevertheless, out of compassion for sentient beings, he frequently entered the village from time to time; having finished his meal and duties within the village, he would depart, thereby inspiring pure faith in many hundreds of thousands of households.”

His retinue was also skilled in transformation and guidance; wherever they went among sentient beings, they preached the Dharma for them, causing many hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"If the assembly belonging to the bhikṣu Sukṛtamati delights in the cultivation of meditative concentration and does not frequently enter villages,
at that time the bhikṣu Sukṛtamati will give rise to an impure mind toward the Dharma-preacher Viśuddhasucarita and his assembly, and say:
'These are indolent bhikṣus who constantly enter villages frequently.'"
He immediately struck the *ghanṭā* to assemble the community of bhikṣus and established a regulation for them, saying:
"None of you shall enter the village.
Then, he addressed his own disciples who were pure and virtuous in conduct, speaking to them as follows:
"You do not skillfully understand conduct and you speak excessively; for what reason do you enter villages so frequently?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, praise and permit dwelling in *āraṇya*. You must not go to the homes of others; you should dwell in the bliss of meditative concentration through reflection."
“O son of good family!

At that time, all the followers of the bhikṣu Viśuddhacāritra did not comply with the instructions and teachings established by the bhikṣu Sucaritamanas; furthermore, they frequently entered villages for the sake of maturing sentient beings.”
"Son of good family!
At that time, after that bhikṣu had left the village, the bhikṣu Sucaritamanas struck the *gandi* to assemble the community of bhikṣus and spoke thus:
'If you enter the village again, you shall not be allowed to dwell together with me in this residence.'"
"O son of a good family!
At that time, the Dharma-preacher Viśuddhacāritra, in order to protect that bhikṣu, addressed his own followers, saying:
'None of you shall enter the village.'"

At that time, all the sentient beings in that village who had been brought to spiritual maturity by that bhikṣu, not seeing those bhikṣus, became filled with feverish distress, and their wholesome dharmas declined.
“O son of good family!

At that time, the Dharma-preacher Viśuddhacāritra, after those three months had passed, departed from his residence and went to another dwelling. Together with his assembly of followers, he again entered villages, cities, towns, and royal capitals; having entered them, he preached the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.”
"Son of good family!

At that time, the bhikṣu Sucaritamanas again saw the Dharma-preacher Viśuddhasucarita frequently entering village houses, and he also saw that assembly, with their natural deportment, entering the homes of others."
Furthermore, they give rise only to impure thoughts, thinking:
"This bhikṣu has evil precepts and broken discipline; since his own person is thus, so too are his followers. What bodhi can there be for this shaven-headed one?"
"This is merely a deceptive fraud.
He then addressed many people, saying:
"This bhikṣu practices in a mixed manner and is far from bodhi; he values gain and offerings, and is defiled by his attachment to the families of others."
“O son of good family!
At that time, the bhikṣu Sucaritamatī died.
However, at the moment of his death, because impure thoughts had arisen toward him and his karma had reached maturity, he fell into the great Avīci hell.”

Having spent ninety-nine koṭis of hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the great hells and having fully experienced all the sufferings of those great hells, they will constantly be subject to slander for sixty-three hundred thousand births;
and though they go forth into homelessness during thirty-three hundred thousand births, they will subsequently fall back into the secular life.

Due to the remaining karmic obstructions from those [previous] actions, he went forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalajvāla; although his lifespan was long, for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years he practiced with diligence as if his head were on fire, yet he still had not attained the patient acceptance that accords with the Path (anulomikī-kṣānti).
Furthermore, for many hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, he was dull-witted due to the remaining effects of that karma.
"Son of good family!
Do not view it otherwise: the monk who preached the Dharma at that time, named Viśuddhacāritra, was none other than you."
Why is this? The Tathāgata Acala was, at that time, the preaching bhikṣu named Viśuddhacāritra.
O son of good family!
At that time, the bhikṣu who preached the Dharma was named Śubhamatī;
do not view him as anyone else.
Why is this? It was I myself who was that bhikṣu preaching the Dharma named Śubhamatī at that time.
Regarding that person, even with respect to the most subtle skillful means, once an impure thought arose within me, I committed this karmic obstruction and fell into the great niraya hell.
“O son of good family!
There is such a subtle karmic obstruction.
O son of good family!”

If there is a bodhisattva who does not wish for such karmic obstructions, they should not contravene the various practices of a second bodhisattva, and they should in all their actions maintain faith and compliance.
One should give rise to this thought:
"I do not know the minds of others; the conduct of sentient beings is likewise difficult to know.
O son of good family!

Because the Tathāgata perceives this meaning, he teaches such a Dharma regarding the *pudgala*; the *pudgala* should not exercise discrimination, for only I am able to discriminate among *pudgalas* and those who resemble me.
O son of good family!

If you wish to protect yourself, you should not select those who act in certain ways, nor should you create obstacles for others; such being the case, you should diligently apply yourself to the Buddha-dharma, practicing mindfulness day and night in accordance with the Dharma.
O son of good family!
A bodhisattva who has set forth with a profound resolve should no longer create obstacles for others, but should instead diligently practice in accordance with and in conformity with [the Dharma].
"O son of good family!
Suppose there were sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, and a bodhisattva were to establish them all in the ten paths of wholesome action;

yet, if another bodhisattva were to go alone to a secluded place and, for even as long as a finger-snap, believe in the path of the single characteristic of all phenomena—whether by questioning about it, discussing it, explaining it, teaching it to others, or reciting it oneself—the merit produced by this would far exceed that of the former."
Why is this? Son of good family!
It is because by means of this path, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas purify their karmic obstructions and, among all sentient beings, remain free from love and hatred, swiftly reaching omniscience.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, regarding what the Buddha has called the purification of karmic obstructions— how, O Bhagavān,
should a bodhisattva purify their karmic obstructions?”
The Buddha said,
"Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who perceives that all phenomena are without karma and without retribution, he shall reach the purification of karmic obstructions."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a bodhisattva who perceives the limit of desire as the limit of reality, they shall reach the purification of karmic obstructions;
if they perceive the limit of hatred and the limit of delusion as the limit of reality, they shall reach the purification of karmic obstructions.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a bodhisattva who perceives all sentient beings as the very realm of nirvāṇa, that person shall reach the purification of karmic obstructions. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī! By means of that conformable vision, their karmic obstructions are purified. Mañjuśrī!
"Sentient beings who do not see the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, and who possess the four inverted minds, cannot transcend this unreal cyclic existence.
When he had spoken thus, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, please explain:
how is it that sentient beings have something to which they cling as an object of vision, such that they cannot transcend cyclic existence?"
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Because sentient beings are attached to ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self,’ they are unable to transcend saṃsāra.”
Why is that? Mañjuśrī!
If one perceives self and other, there is the activity of karma.
Mañjuśrī! Because they lack learning, foolish ordinary beings do not know that all phenomena are ultimately in a state of parinirvāṇa; thus, they perceive a distinction between self and others.
Having seen this, one performs three kinds of actions:
those of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding what does not exist, one grasps at existence and discriminates, thinking, "I have greed, I have hatred, I have delusion."
If he goes forth in the teaching of the Tathāgata, he should form this thought:
"I possess the precepts; my conduct is pure; I shall transcend saṃsāra; I shall attain nirvāṇa; I shall be liberated from suffering."
He further discriminates: "This dharma is wholesome;

this dharma is unwholesome; this dharma is with outflows; this dharma is without outflows; this dharma is to be known; this dharma is to be abandoned; this dharma is to be realized; this dharma is to be cultivated."
That is to say: suffering should be known, its origin should be abandoned, its cessation should be realized, and the path should be cultivated.

Furthermore, one discerns that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, and all conditioned phenomena are ablaze; thus, one thinks: "I should flee from these conditioned phenomena."
When he thus observes the arising [of birth], he develops a sense of weary detachment toward the conceptualization of their conjunction.
With this as his preliminary practice, he forms this thought:
"This suffering should be known."
Regarding those phenomena that ought to be known, he thinks:
"I should abandon the origin [of suffering].
He feels shame, revulsion, and fear toward all phenomena, and he thinks:
"This accumulation should be abandoned.
If one feels shame and revulsion toward these phenomena, they form this thought:
"Cessation should be realized; the Path should be cultivated."
Having analyzed those phenomena, he further understands their cessation, and he thinks:
"This is that cessation which should be realized.
Regarding these phenomena that ought to be realized, he thinks:
"I should cultivate the path.
Thereupon, he goes alone to a secluded place and contemplates all phenomena, attaining *śamatha* and extinguishing discursive thought.

Because he has attained *śamatha*, his mind naturally blossoms and becomes cool and moist amidst all phenomena; he further gives rise to a sense of shame and a mind that finds no delight [in worldly things].
He forms this thought:
"I am liberated from all suffering; there is nothing further to be done.
He considers himself an Arhat and knows it thus.

When they are about to die, they see the place where they will be reborn; they then develop doubt and improper mental states regarding the Buddha’s enlightenment. Because their minds have fallen into doubt, after death they shall fall into the great hells.
"Why is this? Because they fall into conceptualizing all phenomena as being non-arisen, they harbor a mind of disparagement and harm toward the Buddha's bodhi.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one view the Four Noble Truths?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! If one sees that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are unarisen, one knows suffering (*duḥkha*);
if one sees that all conditioned phenomena do not arise, one abandons the origin (*samudaya*).”
Mañjuśrī, if one perceives all phenomena as ultimately in parinirvāṇa, that person realizes cessation;
if one perceives all phenomena as non-existent, that person cultivates the path. Mañjuśrī!

If one views the Four Noble Truths in this way, one does not discriminate among these phenomena as "this is wholesome" or "this is unwholesome," nor does one think, "this should be known," "this should be abandoned," "this should be realized," or "this should be cultivated. That is to say: suffering should be known, its origin should be abandoned, its cessation should be realized, and the path should be cultivated.

Why is this? Because whatever places of passion, hatred, and delusion ordinary worldlings and children are stained by, therein they perceive those phenomena as unarisen, non-existent, unreal, and bound by conceptual construction.
Having seen thus, he neither grasps nor rejects within those phenomena; he sees that all desire, hatred, and delusion are by their very nature like space.

He has no attachment to the three realms; he perceives the three realms as unarisen, seeing them as like an illusion, a dream, an echo, and a shadow, and he views all wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as being like a mirage.
One sees the realm of desire as the realm of nirvāṇa; one sees the realm of hatred as the realm of nirvāṇa;
one sees the realm of delusion as the realm of nirvāṇa.
Seeing all phenomena as having such an intrinsic nature, one then remains free from love and hatred toward all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they perceive neither love nor hatred toward any phenomena; their minds are equal to empty space, and they likewise do not perceive the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha.

Since they do not perceive any phenomena, they have no basis for doubt regarding the Dharma; since they do not harbor doubt, they have no grasping; since there is no grasping, there is no birth; and thus they shall enter nirvana.
Mañjuśrī! Because the Elder Subhūti understands such dharmas, he does not come to prostrate at the feet of the Tathāgata. Why is that?
"He does not even perceive his own body, much less would he perceive the Tathāgata;
such a thing is impossible.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one view the four foundations of mindfulness?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! In future ages there will be bhikṣus who, regarding this impure body, practice the contemplation of the body in accordance with it and call it a foundation of mindfulness;
and regarding feelings that arise and cease, they practice the contemplation of feelings in accordance with them and call it a foundation of mindfulness.”

Seeing that the mind is indeed a phenomenon that arises and a phenomenon that ceases, one contemplates the mind in accordance with that mind; this is called the foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). He speaks thus:

if there is a perception of a whole (*piṇḍasaṃjñā*), that does not exist; if there is a perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), that also does not exist. Within these phenomena, one contemplates phenomena in accordance with those phenomena; this is called the foundation of mindfulness.
When he had spoken thus, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha again:
“World-Honored One,
how further should the four foundations of mindfulness be cultivated?”
The Buddha said:
"It is not necessary, Mañjuśrī!"
“The intentional meaning spoken by the Tathāgata is difficult to understand. Mañjuśrī replied,
“Great Virtuous World-Honored One!”
"However, you should simply explain the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"
If one perceives that one's own body is equal to space, this is the application of mindfulness of the body in accordance with the body within the body.
Mañjuśrī! If one does not apprehend feeling as being either internal, external, or between the two, this is the application of mindfulness of feeling in accordance with feeling within feelings.
Mañjuśrī! If one knows that this mind exists only as a mere designation, this is the application of mindfulness to the mind in accordance with the mind. Mañjuśrī!
If one does not perceive any phenomena as either wholesome or unwholesome, this is the application of mindfulness on phenomena as phenomena within the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī, it is in this way that the four applications of mindfulness should be viewed.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
how should one view the Noble Eightfold Path?”
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! If one sees that all phenomena are without anything that is not equal, are non-dual, and do not create duality—this is right view.”

Mañjuśrī! If one sees all phenomena without conceptualizing them, without variously conceptualizing them, and without universally conceptualizing them—because there is nothing to be seen—this is right conceptualization.
Mañjuśrī! If one sees that all phenomena are inexpressible, because they have been well-cultivated through the equality of expression, this is right speech. Mañjuśrī!
If one sees that all phenomena are without action and without an agent, because no agent can be found, this is right action.
Mañjuśrī! If one neither accumulates nor disperses regarding all phenomena, but lives with right livelihood, this is right livelihood.
Mañjuśrī! Because one does not give rise to nor initiate activity toward any phenomena, this is right effort. Mañjuśrī!
If, among all phenomena, one does not form any thoughts, and having already abandoned the activity of thought, does not recollect them either—this is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Mañjuśrī!

If one sees that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena enters into meditative concentration, being without distraction and without objective support because it is ungraspable—this is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
"Mañjuśrī, in this way the Noble Eightfold Path should be viewed.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
How should one view the five faculties?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! If one has faith that all phenomena are unarisen because they are unarisen by their very nature, this is the faculty of faith. Mañjuśrī!”
If, regarding all phenomena, the mind does not give rise to [conceptual] dispatching because it is free from near and distant perceptions, this is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*). Mañjuśrī!
If one does not form mental intentions toward all phenomena because the nature of objective support is absent, such that mindfulness is not bound, this is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
Mañjuśrī! If one does not recollect or conceptualize any phenomena, because they are unattainable like an illusion—this is the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya). Mañjuśrī!
If one sees that all phenomena are free from arising and free from non-wisdom because their intrinsic nature is empty,
this is the faculty of wisdom. Mañjuśrī,
in this way should the five faculties be viewed.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
how should one view the seven factors of enlightenment?”
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! If one perceives that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and does not form conceptual thoughts, this is the factor of awakening of mindfulness.”

Mañjuśrī! If, having investigated all phenomena, one does not apprehend the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate because they are not established, this is the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Mañjuśrī! If one neither grasps nor rejects the three realms, because of knowing that the perception of realms has been destroyed, this is the factor of enlightenment of diligence. Mañjuśrī!
If, among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one is not bound by joy, because one knows that joy is destroyed by non-joy, this is the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Mañjuśrī! If the mind comes to rest within all phenomena, this is the factor of awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Mañjuśrī! If one knows that the mind cannot be apprehended within all phenomena because it accords with awakening, this is the factor of awakening of concentration (samādhisambodhyaṅga). Mañjuśrī!

Mañjuśrī, if one does not rely upon or dwell in any phenomena, does not cling to or become bound by them, and attains equanimity through not perceiving any phenomena, this is the factor of awakening of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
In this way, one should view the seven factors of awakening.
Mañjuśrī, if there is anyone who thus views the four noble truths, the four foundations of mindfulness, the noble eightfold path, and the five faculties...
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, I shall declare that such a person is called one who has crossed over, one who has reached the further shore,
one who has reached dry land, one who has attained peace, one who has attained fearlessness,
one who has shaken off the dust, one who is without possessions, and one who is free from desire.
One who is free from affliction and unimpeded is called an Arhat; one is called a "Destroyer of Outflows" (Kṣīṇāsrava);
one is called "one who has done what was to be done and whose task is accomplished"; one is called "one who has laid down the heavy burden"; one is called "one who has attained their own benefit";
one is called "one who has exhausted the fetters of existence" (Bhava-saṃyojana), and so on, up to being called "one who has attained mastery over the mind."
One who has reached the other shore is called a śramaṇa, is called a brāhmaṇa, is called one who is able to cross over,
is called one who has crossed over the Vedas, is called a śrotāyaṇa, is called a Buddha,
is called a son of the Buddha, is called a son of Śākya, and is called one who has trampled underfoot the thorns and briars.
They are called those who have cleared away the moats; they are called those who have crossed the moats; they are called those who have extracted the arrowheads;
they are called those who are free from feverish affliction; they are called bhikṣus; they are called noble ones (ārya);
and they are called those whose banners are fulfilled.
“Mañjuśrī! A bhikṣu who is endowed with such patience is able to purify his giving and should receive offerings from the worlds of devas and humans alike.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī!”

A bhikṣu who wishes not to consume the food of the country in vain; who wishes to destroy Māra; who wishes to transcend saṃsāra; who wishes to proceed toward nirvāṇa; who wishes to be liberated from suffering; and who wishes to become a field of merit for pure offerings by gods, humans, and others—should diligently practice and correspond with this Dharma.
When these words were spoken, thirty-two thousand devaputras attained realization within the Dharma; they scattered mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers over the Buddha and spoke these words:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"

If one merely hears this Dharma with their ears, they are considered to have gone forth well within the teaching of the Tathāgata; how much more so for those who, having heard it, take faith and understanding as a condition to practice in accordance with reality?
“Bhagavān!
If those sentient beings were even to hear this teaching, they would attain freedom from overweening pride.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
Please expound the phrases of the dhāraṇī.

By means of this dhāraṇī, may bodhisattvas attain unimpeded eloquence; may they have no fear within even a single sound; may they give rise to all dharmas within the Buddha-dharma; and may they have faith and understanding that all dharmas are the path of a single characteristic.”
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
For that reason, you should listen well!”
I now teach this Dharma-gate, called the "Kīla-phrase" and the "Seed-phrase.
By means of this Dharma-gate, all bodhisattvas shall attain clear illumination regarding all phenomena and swiftly attain the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) within the dharma of non-arising.
Mañjuśrī asked: "What is the dharma-gate of the kīla-phrase and the seed-syllable phrase?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! The single-mindedness of all sentient beings is the seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this the seed-syllable?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! The minds of all sentient beings are entirely non-existent, because no objective referent can be apprehended;
that, Mañjuśrī, is the seed-syllable.”
“The minds of all sentient beings are of one and the same measure;
this is the seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One!”
"For what reason is this a seed-syllable?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"
The minds of all sentient beings are equal in measure to space, because they enter into unattached and impartial conduct;
that is the seed-syllable for this, Mañjuśrī!
"All sentient beings, and even a single sentient being, are seed-syllables. Mañjuśrī asked:
"For what reason are they seed-syllables?"
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! To say that all sentient beings are ‘only one’ is ultimately unarisen and free from names, because neither unity nor difference can be apprehended; that is the seed-syllable.”
"Mañjuśrī! Desire is a kīla-phrase. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this called a ‘kīla-word’?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Desire is immovable, abiding in the dharmadhātu because it does not abide;
it is unshakable because its intrinsic nature is detached.”
That is the kīla phrase.
Mañjuśrī! Hatred is the vajra phrase.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
for what reason is this a vajra-word?”
The Buddha said:
"Mañjuśrī! Hatred cannot be shattered nor can it be severed, just as that vajra is neither shattered nor severed."
"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī! All dharmas are likewise neither broken nor severed, because no phenomena are established; that is this vajra-word."
“Mañjuśrī! Ignorance is a term for wisdom. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this a ‘phrase of wisdom’?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! These very dharmas are extinguished within wisdom and are far removed from non-wisdom; just as that space is neither endowed with wisdom nor endowed with non-wisdom.”
"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!
All phenomena are neither endowed with wisdom nor are they devoid of wisdom."
Because wisdom, ignorance, and that which is to be known are by nature quiescent, that is the phrase for this wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! Form is a kīla-phrase.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
for what reason are these called ‘kīla-words’?”
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Just as that door-peg of the Lord of Gods does not move or waver because it is well-established.”
"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!
All phenomena abide within the dharmadhātu; because they do not abide, they neither go nor come, neither grasp nor relinquish, nor do they perform any activity toward anything else."
Because it abides in non-abiding, that is the *kīla* (stake) phrase.
Mañjuśrī, sensation is the phrase for tranquility.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
for what reason is this called the ‘phrase of tranquility’?”
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!
All sensations are by nature quiescent;
they are neither internal nor external, neither in the east nor in the south, neither in the west nor in the north, neither below nor above, nor within the ten directions.”
Mañjuśrī! If pleasant feeling were internal, sentient beings would be exclusively happy. Mañjuśrī!
Mañjuśrī, if painful feeling were internal, sentient beings would be exclusively suffering. Mañjuśrī,
if neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling were internal, sentient beings would be exclusively deluded.
Mañjuśrī! Therefore, all sensations are neither internal nor external; they cannot be found in the east, the south, the west, the north, below, above, or anywhere within the ten directions.
Therefore, all sentient beings are like grass, trees, and walls; because their fundamental nature is neither born nor extinguished, that is this phrase of tranquility, Mañjuśrī!
“Perception is the seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what reason is this a seed-syllable?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

Conceptualizations arise through discrimination rather than according to reality; they are like an empty fist, resembling a mirage in their own characteristics because their intrinsic nature is devoid of selfhood. This is the seed-syllable for that.
“Mañjuśrī! Practice is the seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this the seed-syllable?
The Buddha said:

“Mañjuśrī! Because of improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise; yet they are already free from all enumeration, being beyond number and surpassing number, like the core of a plantain tree.”
Mañjuśrī! Just as the fruit of a plantain tree is ultimately non-existent— because it cannot be found and its intrinsic nature is unarisen— so it is, so it is.
Mañjuśrī! All phenomena are by their very nature dissociated; because they are already dissociated, that is the seed-syllable for this. Mañjuśrī!
"Consciousness is the seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is this a seed-syllable?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

Consciousness is like the appearance of an illusion—neither arising nor emerging; it is empty, signless, devoid of intrinsic nature, and without characteristics, like space. Because it is based upon the drawing of five fingers, that is the seed-syllable.
“Mañjuśrī! ‘Form’ is a seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is this the seed-syllable?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! Because all forms are non-arisen. Mañjuśrī!”
Just as a reflection is seen yet does not exist, even so, Mañjuśrī!
Although various forms are seen, they do not exist; they are merely a delusion of the eye and a delusion of the mind, for they are false and unreal phenomena. Therefore, that is the seed-syllable.
"Mañjuśrī! Sound is a seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this the seed-syllable?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! All phenomena are without variety and without various characteristics. Mañjuśrī!”
All sounds are non-dual, for all paths of speech are like the resonance of an echo;
therefore, that is the seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī!
Fragrance is a seed-syllable.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
for what reason is this a seed-syllable?”
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! All phenomena are not smelled;
their intrinsic nature is insentient and equal to space, for neither the nose nor the smelling of odors can be apprehended. That is the seed-syllable.”
“Mañjuśrī! Taste is a seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this a seed-syllable?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! The element of taste is itself inconceivable;
taste is unknowable and detached from consciousness, for its primordial nature is free [from conceptualization]. This is the seed-syllable of that.”
“Mañjuśrī! Contact is a seed-syllable. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this a seed-syllable?
The Buddha said:

Regarding all dharmas that are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): they should not be learned, should not be cultivated, should not be contemplated, should not be recollected, should not be dwelled upon, should not be initiated, should not be practiced, should not be abandoned, should not be realized, should not be spoken of, should not be manifested, and should not be sought. Because the intrinsic nature of sentient beings is itself omniscience, that is the *kīla* phrase.

the fact that all sentient beings are endowed with omniscience is the *kīla* phrase.

That all sentient beings are fully endowed with the immeasurable is a *kīla* (stake) phrase.

“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings transcend calculation and are beyond number; if one knows them thus as immeasurable, because they are as immeasurable as space, that is this ‘kīla-word’ (stake-word).”
“World-Honored One!

“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of the term ‘bodhimaṇḍa’?

“World-Honored One!
Do all sentient beings not constantly enter this field?

"So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī! Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!

World-Honored One!”

“World-Honored One!

“World-Honored One!
