Because the mind is said to be difficult to know,
O Devaputra!

Regarding the gateway of sounds, even if a bodhisattva were to be reviled and abused with untruthful words for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they would harbor no mind of anger or obstruction therein.

Furthermore, even for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, if one were to obtain a pure mind and a benevolent intention to provide offerings—respecting all causes and conditions of pleasure such as food, clothing, bedding, and medicines for the sick—he would still harbor no heart of attachment toward them.
"Noble son!

Just as an arhat whose outflows are exhausted never gives rise to craving toward those phenomena that are bases for attachment, nor does he give rise to aversion toward those phenomena that are bases for resentment."
O son of good family!

Through this entrance into the gateway of sound, even if a bodhisattva were to obtain all the causes and conditions for pleasure as offerings throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, no mind of attachment would arise within them.

Even if they were to revile him with words that were not in accordance with reality for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, he would harbor no mind of anger or resentment therein.
O son of good family!
Entering through such gateways of sound, the bodhisattva experiences neither acceptance nor attachment toward gain or loss, defamation or praise, renown or insignificance, suffering or pleasure;
they abide transcending worldly dharmas, like the king of mountains.
When he had spoken thus, the devaputra Padmavikrīḍitajñānābhijña addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva trains, how does he train in the gateway of entering into sounds?”
The Buddha said,
"Son of good family!
Why do you now need to ask about such a matter?"
The devaputra said:
“World-Honored One!

Please explain the wisdom that enters into sounds. If there are bodhisattvas in the future who enter this patience, they should form conceptions of purity, conceptions of faith, and conceptions of love toward it.”
“Having heard these sounds and entered into wisdom, they shall awaken to their own evil and instruct others as well.
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Devaputra Padmavikrīḍitajñānābhijña, saying:
“If that is so, Devaputra, listen well and reflect with right mindfulness; I shall expound this meaning for you.”
The Devaputra Padmavikrīḍitajñānābhijña replied: “So it is!
I am very eager to hear this.”
The Buddha said,

“Devaputra! If there is a bodhisattva who conceives thoughts of transgression and fault regarding sounds of desire, and conceives thoughts of praise and benefit regarding sounds free from desire, then they do not train within the Buddha-dharma.”
To conceive thoughts of fault and transgression regarding sounds of anger, and thoughts of praise and benefit regarding sounds free from anger, is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To conceive thoughts of fault and transgression regarding sounds of delusion, and thoughts of praise and benefit regarding sounds free from delusion, is not to study the Buddha-dharma.
To feel attachment toward the sound of "few desires" and aversion toward the sound of "many desires" means one is not training in the gateway of sounds.
To feel attachment toward the sound of "contentment" and aversion toward the sound of "lack of contentment" means one is not training in the gateway of sounds.
If one feels attraction toward sounds that are concise and aversion toward sounds that are not concise, then one is not training in the gateway of sounds.
To speak briefly in this way, one should know that there is attraction toward sounds of solitude and aversion toward sounds of crowds;
attraction toward the voice of the Buddha and aversion toward the voices of non-Buddhists; [and so forth].
They feel attraction toward the sound of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and aversion toward the sound of what is not the holy life;
they feel attraction toward the sound of the Vinaya and aversion toward the sound of what is not the Vinaya;
they feel attraction toward the sound of purity and aversion toward the sound of afflictions (*kleśa*).
To feel attraction toward pleasant sounds and aversion toward unpleasant sounds is not to train in the gateway of sound.
To feel attraction toward the voice of the fruit [of realization] and aversion toward the voice of ordinary beings is likewise so.
To feel attachment toward pleasant sounds and aversion toward unpleasant sounds;
to feel attachment toward supramundane sounds and aversion toward mundane sounds—
this is not training in the gateway of sounds.
If one feels attraction toward the sound of renunciation and aversion toward the sound of household life, one is not training in the gateway of sounds.
If one feels attraction toward the sound of generosity and aversion toward the sound of stinginess, thereby giving rise to obstructive thoughts, one is not training in the Buddha-dharma.

If one conceives thoughts of praise and benefit toward the sound of "observing the precepts," and thoughts of aversion and obstruction toward the sound of "breaking the precepts," then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
If one conceives thoughts of praise and benefit toward the sound of "patience," and thoughts of obstruction toward the sound of "anger," then one is not studying the Buddha-dharma.
"To speak briefly: if one conceives the notion of praise and benefit toward the sound of diligence, and the notion of obstruction toward the sound of indolence;
if one conceives the notion of praise and benefit toward the sound of meditative concentration, and the notion of obstruction toward the sound of distraction;
if one conceives the notion of praise and benefit toward the sound of wisdom, and the notion of obstruction toward the sound of ignorance, then one does not train in the Buddha-dharma."
To feel attachment toward sounds that are near and aversion toward sounds that are distant is not to train in the gateway of sounds.
To conceive thoughts of fault and transgression regarding the sound of saṃsāra, and thoughts of praise and benefit regarding the sound of nirvāṇa, is not to train in the gateway of sounds.
If one feels aversion toward sounds on this shore and attachment toward sounds on the other shore;
if one conceives thoughts of fault and transgression regarding the sounds of a village, while conceiving thoughts of praise and benefit regarding the sounds of an araṇya;
then one is not training in the gateway of sounds.
To feel attachment toward those who practice alone and aversion toward those who practice in community is not to train in the Buddha’s Dharma.
To feel attachment toward the conduct of monks and aversion toward the conduct of householders;
to feel attachment toward conduct that accords with the monastic rules and aversion toward conduct that does not accord with the monastic rules; [is likewise not to train in the Buddha’s Dharma].
One feels attraction toward pure and sublime conduct and aversion toward that which is not pure and sublime;
one feels attraction toward virtuous conduct and aversion toward unvirtuous conduct;
one feels attraction toward unmixed conduct and aversion toward mixed conduct.
One feels attraction toward conduct free from sensual desire and aversion toward conduct characterized by sensual desire;
one feels attraction toward conduct free from ill will and aversion toward conduct characterized by ill will;
one feels attraction toward conduct free from delusion and aversion toward conduct characterized by delusion.
One feels attraction toward the practice of emptiness and aversion toward the practice of views;
one feels attraction toward the signless and aversion toward signs;
one feels attraction toward the wishless and aversion toward wishes.
To feel attachment toward the conduct of bodhisattvas and aversion toward the conduct of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is to fail to train in the Buddha-dharma.
To disparage the faults of bodhisattvas distances one from bodhi and incurs karmic obstructions.
If one censures another's deportment, one distances oneself from bodhi and also incurs firm karmic obstructions;
if a bodhisattva conceives a sense of inferiority toward another bodhisattva while conceiving a sense of superiority toward themselves, they cause themselves harm and also incur karmic obstructions.
In this way, when a bodhisattva instructs or admonishes another bodhisattva, they should conceive of them as a teacher before providing instruction or admonition.
If a bodhisattva wishes not to abandon awakening, they must not harbor thoughts of inferiority toward other bodhisattvas.
“O son of good family!
For a bodhisattva, there is no single act that severs roots of goodness as much as disparaging a second bodhisattva.

Therefore, if a bodhisattva wishes to protect all roots of goodness, wishes to purify all karmic obstructions, and wishes to swiftly attain unimpeded conduct regarding all dharmas, they should, during each of the three periods of day and night, pay homage to those persons who belong to the Bodhisattvayāna.”
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the sound of desire and the sound of the Buddha are equal in measure; the sound of hatred and the sound of the Buddha are equal; the sound of delusion and the sound of the Buddha are equal; the sound of non-Buddhists and the sound of the Buddha are equal; the sound of few desires and the sound of many desires are equal; the sound of contentment and the sound of discontent are equal; the sound of frugality and the sound of lack of frugality are equal; the sound of delighting in solitude and the sound of dwelling with the multitude are equal; the sound of this shore and the sound of the other shore are equal; the sound of the distant and the sound of the near are equal; the sound of saṃsāra and the sound of nirvāṇa are equal; the sound of the village and the sound of the araṇya are equal; the sound of giving and the sound of stinginess are equal; the sound of upholding the precepts and the sound of breaking the precepts are equal; the sound of malice and the sound of patience are equal; the sound of diligence and the sound of laziness are equal; the sound of distraction and the sound of meditative concentration are equal; and the sound of ignorance and the sound of wisdom are equal.
At that time, the devaputra Padmavikrīḍitajñānābhijña said to the youth Mañjuśrī:
"Mañjuśrī! For what reason and by what causal conditions are they weighed as being equal?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Son of Heaven!
Regarding such a sound of desire, what do you think it is?"
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī, it is my view that the sound of desire is like an echo."
Mañjuśrī said: "Son of Heaven!
Regarding such a sound of the Buddha, what do you think it is?"
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! In my opinion, it is no different from the nature of an echo.”
Mañjuśrī said, “For this reason, they are weighed as being equal.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:
“Mañjuśrī! When you were in a previous life dwelling on the stage of a beginner and had not yet entered such a path of the Dharma, what karmic obstacles did you create?
You may speak of this now.”
“If there are those in future ages who bear the provisional name of ‘bodhisattva,’ upon hearing of such karmic obstructions and evils as these, they should protect themselves.
When he had spoken thus, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Having heard of such karmic obstructions and evils, although they may feel sorrow and fear, they will purify their karmic obstructions and also attain non-obstruction regarding all dharmas.
World-Honored One!

In the past, incalculable eons ago—further beyond the immeasurable, the unfathomable, and the inconceivable—after that time had passed, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Siṃhadundubhisvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Men to be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.

The lifespan of that Tathāgata will be sixty koṭi-nayuta-hundred-thousand years; he will teach the Dharma to tame sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and he will also bring sentient beings to maturity through the three vehicles.
That world is named Great Radiance (*Mahāprabha*).
Within it, whether trees or pillars, they are fashioned from the seven precious jewels.

From those trees such sounds as these emerge: namely, the sound of emptiness, the sound of signlessness, the sound of wishlessness, the sound of non-arising, the sound of non-ceasing, the sound of non-existence, and the sound of formlessness; such sounds as these constantly issue forth.
When that sound issued forth,
those sentient beings realized the Dharma through direct vision.
At that time, during the Tathāgata’s first assembly, there were ninety-nine koṭis of śrāvakas, all of whom were arhats, their minds fully liberated through the wisdom of equality.
In the second assembly, there were ninety-six koṭis of bhikṣus;
in the third assembly, ninety-three koṭis of bhikṣus;
and in the fourth assembly, ninety koṭis of bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats, their minds well-liberated through the wisdom of equality.

The assembly of those bodhisattvas was likewise numerous; they were all fully endowed with the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), well able to give rise to various paths of the Dharma, had made offerings to many hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of Buddhas, their fame was heard throughout hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of Buddha-fields, they had liberated many hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of sentient beings, had attained the *dhāraṇī* of boundless gates, and had produced hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of *samādhis*.
Furthermore, the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had newly begun their practice and first set out on the vehicle were also immeasurable and innumerable.
The adornments of merit in that Tathāgata’s land are so complete that they could never be fully exhausted through speech.
After that Tathāgata has passed into extinction, the True Dharma shall remain for nine million nine hundred thousand years; during that time, the sounds from those trees will no longer arise.
“World-Honored One!
At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Nandendriya who served as a Dharma-preacher.
World-Honored One!”
That Bodhisattva Nandendriya had previously practiced straightforwardness; he did not differentiate in his deportment, did not renounce the world, and was not obstructed by worldly dharmas.

At that time, the faculties of sentient beings were all sharp; they understood upon hearing little and possessed deep faith and understanding. For those sentient beings, he did not praise or speak of few desires, nor did he praise or speak of contentment, frugality, or delighting in solitude;
nor did he praise or speak of dwelling apart from the multitude.
Nor does he manifest the initiation of diligence;

rather, he manifests himself as practicing mixed conduct so that those sentient beings may grasp all phenomena—grasping them through the very nature of desire, grasping them through the very nature of hatred, and grasping them through the very nature of delusion—without any hindrance.
By means of skillful means, he causes those sentient beings to grasp at the single characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Once he has caused them to grasp this through skillful means, there is not a single place among those beings—whether in their conduct or their deportment—in which there is any obstruction of anger.

Having freed his mind from anger and obstruction, he will attain the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) and shall achieve a firm, indestructible, and profound resolve within the teaching of the Tathāgata.
"World-Honored One!
At that time, there will also be a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Jayamati, who likewise serves as a Dharma-preacher."
"Bhagavān!
The Dharma-preacher Jayamati has attained the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, and practices twelve kinds of *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power) merits.
Bhagavān!"
Those who are disciplined by the Bodhisattva Jayamati seize upon the faults and evils of others, and their wisdom wavers.
"World-Honored One!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jayamati was walking through a village for alms and arrived at the house where the Bodhisattva Priyamūla was seeking food."

Because he did not know [the truth], he saw the son of the householder there; he went to where the son of the householder was, and having arrived, he prepared a seat for him. Once seated, he spoke to the son of the householder concerning fewness of desires, contentment, austerity, and the faults of dwelling with a crowd; he praised the joy of solitude and praised not dwelling with a crowd.
Furthermore, in the presence of that householder’s son, he spoke ill of the Bodhisattva Priyamūla, saying:
"That bhikṣu causes many people to fall into perversion."
That bhikṣu causes many people to adopt wrong views.
That bhikṣu is one of mixed conduct; he grasps at desire without hindrance, grasps at hatred without hindrance, grasps at delusion without hindrance, and grasps at all phenomena without hindrance.
The son of the householder, being of sharp faculties and having attained patience, said to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, what do you mean when you speak of 'desire'?
The bhikṣu replied:
"In my opinion, desire is an affliction.
The householder's son said,
"Venerable sir!"
"Is lust internal or external?
The bhikṣu replied,
"Lust is neither internal nor external."
The son of the householder said:
"From where does greed arise?
To what place does it go?"
"Furthermore, where does it abide?
The bhikṣu replied,
"Lust neither comes nor goes, and it has no place of abiding."
The son of the householder said:
"Venerable Sir!

If craving does not exist internally or externally, nor in the eastern direction, nor in the southern, western, or northern directions, nor above, below, or in the four intermediate directions; if it has no place of abiding, yet is not without abiding—[then how can it be abandoned?]"
"Is that craving not itself unarisen?
If there is no arising, how can there be affliction or purification?
At that time, the bhikṣu Vijaya, filled with anger and displeasure, rose from his seat and departed, saying these words:
"That bhikṣu causes many people to grasp things incorrectly.
Because he has not trained in entering into sounds, he feels joy toward the voice of a Buddha and anger toward the voice of a non-Buddhist.
Because one has not trained in entering into sounds, one feels joy toward sounds of pure conduct and anger toward sounds of non-pure conduct.
Because one has not trained in entering into sounds, one feels joy toward sounds that are pure and anger toward sounds that are defiled.
Because they have not trained in entering into sounds, they feel joy toward the voice of the noble fruit and anger toward the voice of an ordinary person.
Because they have not trained in entering into sounds, they feel joy toward pleasant sounds and anger toward painful sounds.
Because they have not trained in entering into sounds, they feel joy toward the sound of those who have left the household life and aversion toward the sound of those who remain at home.
Because they have not trained in entering into sounds, they feel joy toward supramundane sounds and aversion toward mundane sounds.

Because they have not trained in entering the sounds [of the Dharma], they conceive the notion of benefit toward the sound of "generosity" and the notion of obstruction toward the sound of "miserliness.

Because they have not trained within the Buddha-dharma, they conceive the notion of benefit toward the sound of "observance of precepts" and the notion of obstruction toward the sound of "breaking precepts."
"Having emerged from those households where he had begged for alms, he returned to the āraṇya.
Upon reaching his dwelling, he instructed the other bhikṣus to likewise take [the offerings]. Then, seeing the Bodhisattva Nandimūla within the assembly, he spoke these words:
'This bhikṣu causes many people to grasp at what is inverted.'"
This bhikṣu causes many people to adopt wrong views.
This bhikṣu is one of mixed conduct; he grasps at desire without hindrance, and likewise grasps at hatred and delusion without hindrance, as well as grasping at all phenomena without hindrance.
The Bodhisattva Nandendriya thought thus:

"This bhikṣu must have created an obstacle to his karma; I must speak these profound words to him, even to the point of causing him to create the causes for the auxiliary dharmas that assist awakening."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nandendriya, wishing to inspire faith in the assembly, spoke these verses before the community of bhikṣus:
“Desire is said to be nirvāṇa; hatred and delusion are likewise so!”
One should awaken to this Middle Way; the Buddha’s bodhi is inconceivable.
If one discriminates between desire, as well as hatred, delusion, and the like, one is far from that Buddha-bodhi, as distant as heaven is from earth.
If one does not destroy desire and hatred, yet enters into ignorance and perceives awakening,
one is then close to supreme awakening and shall attain patience before long.
Greed and awakening are neither two nor one; they enter into equality and are in union.
If one does not awaken by following this way, that Buddha-awakening will be ever more remote.
Greed neither arises nor ceases; it has never caused affliction or defilement in the mind.
Yet, if there is the notion of a self or the view of attainment, one enters the hells because of that greed.
All dharmas of desire are the dharmas of the Buddha; all dharmas of the Buddha are the dharmas of desire.
These two are a single syllable and devoid of marks; one who knows thus is a Teacher.

If, having discriminated between precepts and their violation, one becomes intoxicated and heedless by exalting oneself on account of the precepts, such a person will not be born in heaven, much less attain bodhi; they merely abide in the view of attaining something for themselves.
If, having discriminated among the afflictions, one constantly delights in relying upon hatred and views;
this path is not the supreme enlightenment, for to dwell upon them is the bondage of an ordinary person.
If one dwells in a hermitage and, having made such distinctions, becomes arrogant and deceives others;
for them there is no awakening and no Buddha-dharma, for they merely abide in the view of a hermitage.
Since they are not seen within the *araṇya* dharma, yet display the deportment of a forest-dweller in the midst of villages;
they are but thieves among devas and asuras—how can there be awakening, or the Buddha-dharma?
If one discriminates that "I shall become a Buddha," they are led by the power of ignorance and lack of wisdom;
all Buddha-dharmas are like space, wherein there is neither grasping nor rejecting.
The practice of awakening is fundamentally non-dual; names, numbers, and sounds are spoken for the sake of people.
If one does not enter into this Dharma, that Buddha-awakening will be ever more remote.
If one seeks awakening, there is no awakening; if one perceives awakening, one is far from awakening.
Within this teaching, one does not reach nirvāṇa, for this dharma, when analyzed, has no reality.
If one conceives envy or delight toward the Buddha-dharma, one will remain far from this awakening of the Buddha;
having already conceived envy for that which is not a real dharma, one shall further undergo suffering and affliction.
If one makes offerings to some while not offering to others, one becomes attached to the dharma of making offerings;
if one knows that these realms are identical and equal, such a person shall become a Buddha, the Honored One among men.
If one has never seen the Buddha or the Buddha-dharma in any variety or at any place, then one is unstained by all phenomena;
having awakened to bodhi, one has destroyed Māra.
If one wishes to deliver all sentient beings, yet never conceives of that realm of sentient beings;
seeing that all phenomena are equal to nirvana—only such a person becomes a World-Honored One!
Whether one speaks of non-Buddhists as having evil intent, or speaks of the Buddhas as being superior persons—there is no difference between these two; he who knows this is a guide.
If one awakens to bodhi yet there is nothing to be awakened to, and if one knows thus yet there is nothing known;
if Buddhas and non-Buddhas are not distinguished as being equal to a Buddha—this non-discrimination is the supreme among men.
The Buddha has never awakened to bodhi, and there have never been sentient beings who were liberated;
ordinary people conceptualize where no phenomena exist, and thus they remain far, far removed from the Buddha-dharma.
If conditioned phenomena were not conditioned, their numerical count would never exist;
if there were no number, even calculation would be absent—these skillful means do not speak of duality.
If there are no sentient beings, there is no accomplishment; one does not perceive the Buddha-dharma as being truly existent.
As the Buddha is, so too are all sentient beings; he who knows thus touches upon enlightenment.
If you wish to awaken to supreme bodhi, do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the phenomena of desire;
for the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena of desire are themselves the inconceivable virtues of the Buddha.
If one has never previously awakened within the Buddha-dharma, and does not give rise to the mind for the Bodhi of the Buddha;
if there is no difference between Bodhi and the mind—those who know thus become leaders.
If one exalts oneself by means of the bodhicitta, thinking with discriminative thought, "I shall become a Buddha," then for such a person there is neither bodhi nor the Buddha-dharma;
they have thus abandoned the seal of the self-nature of this Dharma.
If one thinks, "I wish to liberate sentient beings," one is a fool attached to the notion of a "sentient being.
What is called a "sentient being" has no inherent existence as a sentient being; awakening does not abide within sentient beings.
If one sees sentient beings thus terrified, boundless fear will arise within them;
knowing that the words of all sentient beings are like echoes from mountains, such a person is supreme among men.
If one sees that sentient beings are ultimately liberated, Always free from greed, hatred, delusion, and the like;
That sentient beings are quiescent and eternally in great stillness— One who knows thus becomes a Guide.
Craving is neither internal nor external; it has no dependence upon any direction.
Having analyzed all phenomena as lacking reality, one sees that the notion of "self" is merely what deludes the ordinary person.
Like an echo, like a phantom, like a mirage, Like the son of a barren woman, and like a dream;
Just as the various afflictions are invisible, Ordinary beings wander in transmigration due to ignorance.
If one seeks afflictions, they will exist; therefore, choose with right mindfulness and do not be indolent.
Without discriminating between the path and afflictions, one touches the non-conceptual stage of bodhi.
If ordinary beings fear the dharma of emptiness, they shall remain far from the Buddha-dharma;
if they have no doubt regarding the dharma of emptiness, they shall attain supreme enlightenment.
If one discriminates objects through verbal expressions, both the expression and its meaning are inconceivable;
yet, becoming stained by names and the rewards of profit, one claims for oneself that one contemplates the Way without doubt.
Without regarding the words spoken as mere names, one perceives that the *araṇya* has a place where it dwells;
yet, having already distinguished between few desires and contentment, one is once again dragged away by the power of craving.
If a person flees from the phenomena of desire, they cannot escape those very phenomena;
if one can correctly awaken to the reality of the phenomena of desire, they will see the Dharma and thus be free from desire.
Though they guard the prohibitive precepts for a long night, and give rise to meditative concentration for boundless eons,
they are not liberated within this Buddha’s teaching, because they do not awaken to this true reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If one realizes that these phenomena are non-existent, one will have no attachment among all phenomena;
not discriminating between precepts and their violation, one is liberated from the realm of ordinary beings' views of existence.
If one sees that upholding the precepts is always without precepts, and if one realizes that the meaning of the precepts is the dharma of breaking them;
then that which is "breaking the precepts" cannot be found, for such is the realization of the characteristics of the practice of the precepts.
The inconceivable dharmas possessed by the Dharma King, through millions of skillful means, transform sentient beings;
by a single skillful means he causes them to enter this awakening, which is tranquil and free from outflows.
Ordinary beings fall into a great downfall after hearing the teachings on the supreme Dharma;
yet it is without action, without substance, and without marks—a single path of skillful means, empty of intrinsic nature.
Though born into a noble family and delighting in sensual pleasures, having heard the Dharma, he was not startled or terrified;
yet, without having gone forth under this teaching, he became arrogant and held views of self-elevation.
All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the ten directions!
Great Sages and Lords who dwell in the world to bring benefit;
having realized that all phenomena are like space, they attain awakening through the non-arising and non-activity of dharmas.
Lacking knowledge yet conceiving the notion of purity, they hear this true Dharma and are struck with terror;
for koṭis of eons they shall undergo manifold sufferings, constantly experiencing a portion of suffering without interruption.
When these verses were spoken, thirty thousand devaputras attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas;
eighteen thousand bhikṣus, through non-attachment, had their minds liberated from all outflows.
Immediately the earth split open, and the Bodhisattva Vijñāna fell dead into the Great Wailing Hell (*mahāraurava-niraya*).
Due to that karmic obstruction, for hundreds of thousands of *koṭi* eons within the great hells, he underwent various most grievous sufferings and poisons.
Having received [this karma], for seventy hundred thousand births they will constantly suffer slander.
For many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, they shall not hear the name of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Later, he encountered a Tathāgata and went forth in his teaching, yet he took no delight in it.
After having gone forth during sixty hundred thousand lifetimes, he repeatedly broke his precepts and returned to secular life.
Due to those remaining karmic obstructions, he has lived with dull faculties throughout many hundreds of thousands of births.
At that time, the Dharma-preacher known as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhikṣu Priyamūla has now realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening and currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.

In the eastern direction, beyond hundreds of thousands of koṭis of buddha-fields, in the world-system called Ratnacitra, resides and teaches the Dharma the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Guhyavimalāntarātapatejorājaśrī.
"At that time, the one named the bhikṣu Śreṣṭhamati who expounded the Dharma was none other than myself acting as the Dharma-preacher, the bhikṣu Śreṣṭhamati.
World-Honored One!"
While I was experiencing such afflictions and dwelling in such a state, because I had not yet entered this path of the Dharma, I underwent such suffering.

Within that which is without suffering, I conceptualized suffering and perceived it through inversion. Therefore, whether one has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Śrāvaka vehicle, those who do not wish for such karmic obstructions and do not wish for such suffering should not disparage or reject any of the various teachings, nor should they disparage that True Dharma; furthermore, they should not harbor anger or create obstacles toward any single part of it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī,
when you heard those verses at that time, what superior activity did they bring about?”
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!

Because I heard those verses, I arose from that karmic obstruction; having wandered and transmigrated everywhere, I attained profound patience (*gambhīra-kṣānti*) regarding all states, and having attained decisive patience, I am able to skillfully expound the profound Dharma.”
The Buddha said,
“Mañjuśrī! By whose spiritual power is there such recollection of karmic obstructions created over such a vast expanse of time?”
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
Whatever bodhisattvas think, reflect upon, or attend to in accordance with [the Dharma], all of that is the Tathāgata’s spiritual power.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
All such dharmas are the original nature of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"If one attains the ten powers of a Tathāgata, it is equal in measure to hearing this;
if one attains patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, it is equal in measure to hearing this."
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the fruit of hearing this Dharma-text is inconceivable.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!"
It is as you have said.
The fruit of hearing this fundamental dharma is inconceivable; however, the Tathāgata does not record or declare it. Why is this?
Those who do not practice with diligence are unworthy persons; having heard this, they will not believe or understand it. Mañjuśrī!
This is the entrance into all dharmas.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

You should uphold this Dharma-text so that, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is in decline, it may reach the hands of many people, preventing Māras and the gods who are Māra’s followers from finding an opportunity to interfere.”
At that time, in order to sustain this root of the Dharma, the World-Honored One gazed thus without interruption to his left and right.
Having so observed, at that moment, the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, shook in six ways.
At that time, the World-Honored One had already upheld this root of the Dharma;
likewise, all other Buddha-Bhagavāns in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River also uphold this root of the Dharma.

When this fundamental discourse on the Dharma was being taught, even more beings than the sands of the Ganges multiplied tenfold in the ten directions attained patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena; those who realized and saw the Dharma were even more numerous than that—how much more so, then, those who abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, or the stage of no-more-learning?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the name of this Dharma-text?”
"How should I uphold it?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"This fundamental teaching is named 'The Non-Revolution of All Dharmas'; this name should be upheld.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the youth Mañjuśrī rejoiced; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, the devaputra Padmavikrīḍitajñānābhijña, and the other devaputras, along with that assembly of great Bodhisattvas, and the gods, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted.
